b: Based on a novel by Charles Willeford, whose Cockfighter and The Woman Chaser were adapted into cult films, Miami Blues is an eminently appealing, if unassuming, neo-noir leavened by a streak of black humor. Essentially a three-hander character piece, writer-director George Armitage’s film focuses on the exploits of career criminal Frederick J. Frenger Jr. (Alec Baldwin), who prefers to go by Junior; gruff homicide detective Sgt. Hoke Moseley (Fred Ward), who’s soon hot on Junior’s trail; and the earnest, if not especially bright, call girl Susie Waggoner (Jennifer Jason Leigh), with whom Junior takes up in a peculiar parody of domestic bliss.

On arrival at Miami Airport, Junior’s first bit of mischief consists of breaking the fingers of a pesky Hare Krishna, which inexplicably results in the man’s death from shock. From there, Junior’s crime spree escalates in frequency and intensity, which is only compounded after he pays a surprise visit to Moseley’s home, beating him unconscious and seizing his badge, gun, and dentures. It’s that last bit of business that gives you some idea of the film’s offbeat sensibilities. Armitage came out of the “Roger Corman film school” in the early ’70s, where he specialized in exploitation movies with a political subtext like Private Duty Nurses, and he peppers Miami Blues with unexpected shifts in tone and narrative direction.

Miami Blues gets a major boost from its central trio of actors. Baldwin’s chiseled good looks and movie-star charisma feed into his character’s allure, but there’s ice in Junior’s veins, and Baldwin expertly navigates Junior’s mercurial nature. Leigh gives a wonderful warmth to the naïve Susie, allowing just the right amount of bruised suspicion and native intelligence to glimmer through, painting the portrait of a woman who expects little out of life because that’s all it’s ever offered her. And Ward fairly oozes world-weary sarcasm, and he’s got those dentures (and, more importantly, their absence) to play around with as a choice bit of actorly business.

Miami Blues cynically explores the overlap between the world of the cop and the criminal. One of the things that Junior does is use Moseley’s badge to horn in on the weekly graft that Susie’s former pimp, Pablo (José Pérez), pays out to a vice cop, Sgt. Frank Lackley (Paul Gleason), then arrange for the money to be delivered to Moseley’s lodgings. It’s an amusing little setup that’s intended as nothing more than further harassment for Moseley. Junior also uses the badge to foil a number of crimes, taking the proceeds for himself, and, at one point, he even loots a convenience store window after chasing off the prospective burglar.

These amusing incidents lull us into a false sense of complacency (not to mention complicity) with Junior’s criminality. That is, until everything comes crashing down during his encounter with an overly cautious coin dealer, Edie Wulgemuth (Shirley Stoler). If, in a metaphorical sense, we’re Junior’s accomplices, then Susie has been turned into a literal one, and it rests on her moral compass where to draw the line with her assistance. This development gives Susie a real moral arc, allowing her to show more resolve than she has until then. The epilogue has her giving a rueful elegy for Junior. Sure, he might have been a murderous sociopath, but he always ate everything she put in front of him. What else can you ask from a man?

Radiance’s 2023 Blu-ray of Miami Blues was sourced from an older high-definition master, and this new 4K transfer, presented in Dolby Vision HDR, is a marked step up. The vibrant splashes of red found throughout the film are more intense than before, and there’s an even greater range between the pastel shades that dominate its color palette. Image clarity and depth are consistently impressive, both in close-ups, such as when Junior gets his fingers chopped off, and in wide shots of Miami exteriors. Fortunately, none of this comes at the expense of the film grain, which is tight and even and, per Radiance’s notes, unaffected by any grain management. The uncompressed stereo audio is well balanced, allowing the ambient sounds to fill out the background without ever overwhelming the dialogue, which comes through clean as a whistle.

The big bonus here is nearly half an hour’s worth of interviews with actors Alec Baldwin and Jennifer Jason Leigh, recorded in 2015. They talk about where their careers were at when they made Miami Blues, their characters’ motivations and chemistry, and the extent to which director George Armitage allowed them to improvise. Baldwin describes his character as “a baby with a big gun,” and offers an interesting take on straight male characters in the movies of Jonathan Demme, who acted as producer here. Leigh discusses the effects that the release of this film and Last Exit to Brooklyn had on her career and extols the virtues of the script.

Elsewhere, in an interview recorded in 2022 for Radiance’s earlier Blu-ray release of the film, pulp crime expert Maxim Jakubowski discusses the life and career of Charles Willeford, offering plenty of insight into how the novelist’s experiences during the Great Depression shaped his work and how he fits into the same tradition of crime fiction as David Goodis and Jim Thompson. In a separate interview, also from 2022, critic David Jenkins talks about Armitage’s working relationship with Demme and how both men came out of the Roger Corman school of filmmaking. A trailer and an image gallery are also included, and rounding out the package is a 48-page booklet featuring an interview with Armitage, pieces on Baldwin and Fred Ward, and a new essay by critic Glenn Kenny that delves into the legacy of Willeford and his Hoke Moseley character, and how Armitage’s film successfully adapts them for the big screen.
Radiance’s 4K upgrade of Miami Blues is a solid improvement over the label’s own 2023 Blu-ray, especially in terms of image quality, making this the film’s definitive home-video release.

Score:
